messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Autodiff Methods
parts:
Bob,

Currently there's a big difference between calling first-order and higher-order autodiff.

First-order autodiff (i.e. gradients) are called using grad_log_prob defined in src/stan/model/util.hpp,

double log_prob_grad(const M& model,
Eigen::VectorXd& params_r,
Eigen::VectorXd& gradient,
std::ostream* msgs = 0)

Higher-order autodiff, however, are all called using functionals defined in src/stan/agrad/autodiff.hpp, for example

grad_tr_mat_times_hessian(
const F& f,
const Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& x,
const Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,Eigen::Dynamic>& M,
Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& grad_tr_MH)

From an API perspective the former is much nicer as it avoids having to create a functional to wrap models
-- why wasn't this pattern repeated for the higher-order methods?

At the very least it would be much less confusing if the patterns were unified. I'm guessing a move to functions everywhere,
in which case I'd much prefer to define a generic functional as well as wrappers to the autodiff code that take in a model
to hide the call to the functional.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Autodiff Methods
parts:
On 12/17/13, 3:50 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Bob,
>
> Currently there's a big difference between calling first-order and higher-order autodiff.
>
> First-order autodiff (i.e. gradients) are called using grad_log_prob defined in src/stan/model/util.hpp,
>
> double log_prob_grad(const M& model,
> Eigen::VectorXd& params_r,
> Eigen::VectorXd& gradient,
> std::ostream* msgs = 0)
>
> Higher-order autodiff, however, are all called using functionals defined in src/stan/agrad/autodiff.hpp, for example
>
> grad_tr_mat_times_hessian(
> const F& f,
> const Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& x,
> const Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,Eigen::Dynamic>& M,
> Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& grad_tr_MH)
>
> From an API perspective the former is much nicer as it avoids having to create a functional to wrap models

Terminologically in C++, a "functional" is something that takes functions
as arguments., whereas a "functor" is a class that defines a function.
So in the above, grad_tr_mat_times_hessian is a functional, and the
f passed in is a functor (though it'll also accept other ways of passing
in functions). There's a very nice discussion in Vandevoorde and Josuttis.
> -- why wasn't this pattern repeated for the higher-order methods?

I find the latter much nicer. It's much more modular in that
the model only defines the log prob. If I had it to do over,
I'd eliminate the log_prob_grad method from the models rather than
the other way around.
> At the very least it would be much less confusing if the patterns were unified.
Absolutely.
> I'm guessing a move to functions everywhere,

How well you know me!

We're also going to have to address compile times. If every model or
the command winds up having to compile the model for all types, it's
going to be slow.

> in which case I'd much prefer to define a generic functional as well as wrappers to the autodiff code that take in a model
> to hide the call to the functional.

That's how I imagined it going. The subtlelty here is that we
need to bind the print stream and functionally abstract (in the
lambda function sense) on the parameter vector.

The most abstracted way to do this would be with factory function
that mapped a const model pointer and ostream to a functor. Or
you could just use the functor class directly. Or you could just
use bind or one of its generalizations in Boost.

- Bob

parts:
> Terminologically in C++, a "functional" is something that takes functions
> as arguments., whereas a "functor" is a class that defines a function.
> So in the above, grad_tr_mat_times_hessian is a functional, and the
> f passed in is a functor (though it'll also accept other ways of passing
> in functions). There's a very nice discussion in Vandevoorde and Josuttis.
I can never remember the order -- especially given the definitions in math.

> We're also going to have to address compile times. If every model or
> the command winds up having to compile the model for all types, it's
> going to be slow.

Can we just split up the autodiff.hpp into first, second, and third order files?
Then we'd only include and build what we need.

> That's how I imagined it going. The subtlelty here is that we
> need to bind the print stream and functionally abstract (in the
> lambda function sense) on the parameter vector.
>
> The most abstracted way to do this would be with factory function
> that mapped a const model pointer and ostream to a functor. Or
> you could just use the functor class directly. Or you could just
> use bind or one of its generalizations in Boost.

I've been doing this,

template <typename M>
struct _softabs_fun {

const M& _model;
std::ostream* _o;

_softabs_fun(M& m, std::ostream* out): _model(m), _o(out) {};

template <typename T>
T operator()(Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& x) const {
return _model.template log_prob<true, true, T>(x, _o);
}

};

which is readily thrown somewhere in autodiff or model/util, depending
on which way we want the dependency to go (probably the latter?).

Then the wrappers would just be calling the functor.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Autodiff Methods
parts:
On 12/17/13, 5:00 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> Terminologically in C++, a "functional" is something that takes functions
>> as arguments., whereas a "functor" is a class that defines a function.
>> So in the above, grad_tr_mat_times_hessian is a functional, and the
>> f passed in is a functor (though it'll also accept other ways of passing
>> in functions). There's a very nice discussion in Vandevoorde and Josuttis.
>
> I can never remember the order -- especially given the definitions in math.

I first learned the word in Lisp, then in category theory, and
only after that in C++. Language gets awfully overloaded.

Wikipedia doesn't agree with my definition of "functional", redirecting
to:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functor_(C%2B%2B)

>> We're also going to have to address compile times. If every model or
>> the command winds up having to compile the model for all types, it's
>> going to be slow.
>
> Can we just split up the autodiff.hpp into first, second, and third order files?
> Then we'd only include and build what we need.

autodiff.hpp isn't the issue. It's that we have to make
a compile-time decision about what to build. So if there's
an option in the compiled command to use third order, we need
to compile it.

I haven't figured out how to get around this issue. The
fundamental problem is that the model's templated log prob
function has to get instantiated at compile time in all the
ways it might be used at run time.

>> That's how I imagined it going. The subtlelty here is that we
>> need to bind the print stream and functionally abstract (in the
>> lambda function sense) on the parameter vector.
>>
>> The most abstracted way to do this would be with factory function
>> that mapped a const model pointer and ostream to a functor. Or
>> you could just use the functor class directly. Or you could just
>> use bind or one of its generalizations in Boost.
>
> I've been doing this,
>
> template <typename M>
> struct _softabs_fun {
>
> const M& _model;
> std::ostream* _o;
>
> _softabs_fun(M& m, std::ostream* out): _model(m), _o(out) {};
M& should be const here.

> template <typename T>
> T operator()(Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& x) const {
> return _model.template log_prob<true, true, T>(x, _o);
> }
>
> };
>

Exactly what I had in mind for the functor. (Please don't put an "_" before
a structure name. We're trying to move away from initial "_", which are
technically not allowed (though tend not to cause problems other than when
followed by a single capital letter). And I'd like to reserve suffix "_"
for member variables in classes.)

> which is readily thrown somewhere in autodiff or model/util, depending
> on which way we want the dependency to go (probably the latter?).

Definitely the latter. We do not want autodiff.hpp to depend on our models
or vice-versa, so it should go in model/util.
> Then the wrappers would just be calling the functor.

Right.

What I was suggesting is a factory function that does the type inference
for you:

template <typename M>
inline softabs_fun<M>
as_functor(const M& m, std::ostream* out) {
return softabs_fun<M>(m,o);
}

It only saves you having to include the model parameter.
It'd be nice if we could do this and keep softabs_fun<M>
anonymous. To do that, we could use bind:

http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/functional/bind/

I like how they documented the return type!


- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Autodiff Methods
parts: How about this going into model/util.hpp:

template <typename M>
struct _softabs_fun {

const M& _model;
std::ostream* _o;

_softabs_fun(M& m, std::ostream* out): _model(m), _o(out) {};

template <typename T>
T operator()(Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& x) const {
return _model.template log_prob<true, true, T>(x, _o);
}

};

template <class M>
stan::model::grad_tr_mat_times_hessian(
const M& model,
const Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& x,

const Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,Eigen::Dynamic>& X,
Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& grad_tr_MH,
std::ostream* msgs = 0) {

stan::agrad::grad_tr_mat_times_hessian(_softabs_fun<M>(model, msgs), x, X, grad_tr_MH);

}

with better names, etc (although I hate using a suffix _ to denote members -- it's incredibly easy to miss.
I always liked the m/f prefix, but that was for CamelCase).

We can also add the intermediate for type inference, but I can't see a strong argument
for adding it at the moment.

> In the use case, I think at least one of the log_prob
> calls should get the error messages turned on, but they
> don't all need to be turned on.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>> On 12/17/13, 6:13 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> How about this going into model/util.hpp:
>>
>>     template <typename M>
>>     struct _softabs_fun {
>>
>>       const M& _model;
>>       std::ostream* _o;
>>
>>       _softabs_fun(M& m, std::ostream* out): _model(m), _o(out) {};
>>
>>       template <typename T>
>>       T operator()(Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& x) const {
>>         return _model.template log_prob<true, true, T>(x, _o);
>>       }
>>
>>     };
>>
>>     template <class M>
>>     stan::model::grad_tr_mat_times_hessian(
>>                  const M& model,
>>                  const Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& x,
>>                  const Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,Eigen::Dynamic>& X,
>>                  Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& grad_tr_MH,
>>                  std::ostream* msgs = 0) {
>>
>>         stan::agrad::grad_tr_mat_times_hessian(_softabs_fun<M>(model, msgs), x, X, grad_tr_MH);
>>
>>     }
>>
>> with better names, etc (although I hate using a suffix _ to denote members -- it's incredibly easy to miss.
>> I always liked the m/f prefix, but that was for CamelCase).
>>
>> We can also add the intermediate for type inference, but I can't see a strong argument
>> for adding it at the moment.
>>
>>> On Dec 17, 2013, at 5:57 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>> On 12/17/13, 5:00 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>>>>> Terminologically in C++, a "functional" is something that takes functions
>>>>> as arguments., whereas a "functor" is a class that defines a function.
>>>>> So in the above, grad_tr_mat_times_hessian is a functional, and the
>>>>> f passed in is a functor (though it'll also accept other ways of passing
>>>>> in functions).  There's a very nice discussion in Vandevoorde and Josuttis.
>>>>
>>>> I can never remember the order -- especially given the definitions in math.
>>>
>>> I first learned the word in Lisp, then in category theory, and
>>> only after that in C++.  Language gets awfully overloaded.
>>>
>>> Wikipedia doesn't agree with my definition of "functional", redirecting
>>> to:
>>>
>>>  http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functor_(C%2B%2B)
>>>
>>>>> We're also going to have to address compile times.  If every model or
>>>>> the command winds up having to compile the model for all types, it's
>>>>> going to be slow.

>>>> Can we just split up the autodiff.hpp into first, second, and third order files?

>>>
>>> autodiff.hpp isn't the issue.  It's that we have to make
>>> a compile-time decision about what to build.  So if there's
>>> an option in the compiled command to use third order, we need
>>> to compile it.
>>>
>>> I haven't figured out how to get around this issue.  The
>>> fundamental problem is that the model's templated log prob
>>> function has to get instantiated at compile time in all the
>>> ways it might be used at run time.
>>>
>>>>> That's how I imagined it going.  The subtlelty here is that we
>>>>> need to bind the print stream and functionally abstract (in the
>>>>> lambda function sense) on the parameter vector.
>>>>>
>>>>> The most abstracted way to do this would be with factory function
>>>>> that mapped a const model pointer and ostream to a functor.  Or
>>>>> you could just use the functor class directly.  Or you could just
>>>>> use bind or one of its generalizations in Boost.

>>>>
>>>>     template <typename M>

>>>>
>>>>       const M& _model;

>>> M& should be const here.
>>>
>>>>       template <typename T>

>>>>         return _model.template log_prob<true, true, T>(x, _o);
>>>>       }
>>>>
>>>>     };
>>>
>>> Exactly what I had in mind for the functor.  (Please don't put an "_" before
>>> a structure name.  We're trying to move away from initial "_", which are
>>> technically not allowed (though tend not to cause problems other than when
>>> followed by a single capital letter).  And I'd like to reserve suffix "_"
>>> for member variables in classes.)
>>>
>>>> which is readily thrown somewhere in autodiff or model/util, depending
>>>> on which way we want the dependency to go (probably the latter?).
>>>
>>> Definitely the latter.  We do not want autodiff.hpp to depend on our models
>>> or vice-versa, so it should go in model/util.
>>>
>>>> Then the wrappers would just be calling the functor.
>>>
>>> Right.
>>>
>>> What I was suggesting is a factory function that does the type inference
>>> for you:
>>>
>>>  template <typename M>
>>>  inline softabs_fun<M>
>>>  as_functor(const M& m, std::ostream* out) {
>>>    return softabs_fun<M>(m,o);
>>>  }
>>>
>>> It only saves you having to include the model parameter.
>>> It'd be nice if we could do this and keep softabs_fun<M>
>>> anonymous.  To do that, we could use bind:
>>>
>>>  http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/functional/bind/
>>>
>>> I like how they documented the return type!
>>>
>>>
>>> - Bob

Dan,

What kind of tests do you want to see for these interfaces?  Just that they don't throw exceptions (for a Stan model using only simple manipulations at the moment) or actual verification of the gradients?  Or something else?

Use case as in the samplers or tests?

Samplers.


Perhaps we could have a flag for stanc that would control whether we use a higher order auto-diff or not. Then we'd include one command.hpp or similar for just HMC and another for higher order?
